NATURE CLUB CLASS · ANIMALS

The deeper animal deck.

Twenty-two spotter sheets walk the wild in study order — the birds first, then the water from shore to deep, the small crews that run the world, the fur families and their famous cousins, and the wild homes of six habitats — and every tile below opens its own spotter lesson a kid can follow.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Every animal group — with a spotter lesson on its card.

The Nature Club Animals class is the deeper deck: where Animal Categories teaches the big families, this one goes specialist — birds of prey, crustaceans, pollinators, the dog family, rodents, and the wild homes from grassland to mountaintop. Twenty-two spotter sheets, each with four labeled animals, and each card opens a simple lesson a kid can follow: what the group is, who belongs, how to tell the look-alikes apart, and one way to spot them on a real walk.

The walks run in study order on purpose. The birds come first — hunters before singers; then the water, from the shore to the deep; then the small crews that run the world; the fur families with their famous cousins; and the wild homes, six addresses from grassland to cave to mountaintop. The age pills lean Ages 4–5 on purpose too: this is the step-up deck, and the friendliest five cards ride Ages 3+ for confident younger spotters.

THE CLASS GAME

The Spotter’s Walk: one card, one walk, one met animal.

Take one card on your walk — garden-birds on any day, birds-of-prey for the park with the big trees, river-animals for the stream. The job is simple: spot ONE real creature that belongs to the card’s family, and watch it long enough to say one true thing about it. At home, draw what you met next to the card version and write the date. A notebook of met animals is the Nature Club badge of honor — one page per walk, no rush, and the deck decides where next week’s walk goes.

SAME ANIMAL, TWO NAMES

Reindeer and caribou. Both are right.

Animals carry their names across oceans like passports — and this class says so out loud. The reindeer of Lapland is the caribou of Canada and Alaska — same animal, two names. The moose is called the elk in Britain. A shrimp in America is a prawn in Britain. And the buzzard is the trickiest of all: in North America it means a vulture, but in Britain it means a hawk — one word, two birds, and this class teaches both. Whichever your family says, your child hears both — and learns early that animals, like words, come in kinds.

Age ranges are a guide, not a test. The age pill on every card is an honest hint: this is the deeper deck, so most cards ride Ages 4–5 — but the friendliest groups (garden birds, the seashore, the river, the pollinators, the dog family) ride Ages 3+. Start where your child’s curiosity already points; the card in their hand is always the right card.
